title: DOC: clarify fromstring requires sep argument

labels.name: sustain-2026
labels.description: Issues reserved for NumFOCUS Sustaining Open Source Series 2026

body:
### PR summary
Addresses one issue mentioned in #27038, which describes that `np.fromstring`'s documentation doesn't match its behavior when omitting `sep` or passing in `sep=''` (the binary mode behavior was removed in release 2.3.0).

I updated the `fromstring` docs by:
- Removing mention of binary mode from the `dtype` argument, since the functionality was removed
- Removing "optional" from the `sep` argument, and clarifying that it must not be empty
- Switching the `deprecated` callout to a `versionchanged` callout
- Updating the `ValueError` condition
  - The previous condition references binary mode [error checks](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/a98529dfd92d73fd4d40ebaaf285cf2463bb92b1/numpy/_core/src/multiarray/ctors.c#L3895-L3913), but the binary mode [guard](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/a98529dfd92d73fd4d40ebaaf285cf2463bb92b1/numpy/_core/src/multiarray/multiarraymodule.c#L2365) makes this impossible to reach

I also updated the `ValueError` message itself to clearly state that `sep` is required and must not be empty.

Hi! I'm Michael from Bloomberg, participating in the NumFOCUS Open Source program. I use NumPy mostly for personal projects nowadays, but have used it for work and school projects in the past.

I asked Claude Opus `5.5` to be very concise in providing some reproducers that I've verified myself below the fold for `count_nonzero` and `lexsort`. <details>

```python
import numpy as np
```

```python
# expected 1, got 0

# spurious MemoryError

# segfault
```

title: ENH: extremely large single field size dtype support
body:
I suspect this is already known, but I'm not seeing this clearly expressed in open/closed issues? For context the reproducer below came up in an in person discussion with @braxtoncuneo at a meeting at Vanderbildt University, where he was explaining that this limitation was causing some friction in the context of passing data from GPU to CPU (working with NumPy in numba specifically). If this were possible to do, they could store all of their state in a single "struct" and it would make things easier.

I'm not making a comment on whether this should be supported, but passing along some feedback from researchers in case the core team feedback might be helpful.

The single field size case is problematic:

```python
>>> kind = [("x", np.float64, 2**28)]
>>> kind_dtype = np.dtype(kind)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-22>", line 1, in <module>
    kind_dtype = np.dtype(kind)
ValueError: invalid shape in fixed-type tuple: dtype size in bytes must fit into a C int.
```

The aggregated size case is "fine" it seems, even when it exceeds the sum total size of the reproducer above:

```python
>>> kind = [("x", np.float64, 2**28 - 1), ("y", np.float64, 1000)]
>>> kind_dtype = np.dtype(kind)
```

title: DEP: Deprecate np.dot when a.ndim >= 2 and b.ndim > 2

labels.name: sustain-2026
labels.description: Issues reserved for NumFOCUS Sustaining Open Source Series 2026

body:
Closes #31725

### PR summary

**What problem does this PR solve?**

When `a.ndim >= 2` and `b.ndim > 2`, `np.dot()` and `ndarray.dot()` place `b`'s leading dimensions in the middle of the result shape. For example:

```python
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((4, 3, 5))
np.dot(a, b).shape  # (2, 4, 5) - the 4 ends up in the middle
```

Most users expect either `(2, 5)` (like regular matrix multiplication) or `(4, 2, 5)` (batch dimension at front, like `@`/`matmul`). The interleaved result `(2, 4, 5)` is surprising and rarely intended.

**Ecosystem research:** We checked 9 downstream libraries (scipy, scikit-learn, astropy, pandas, xarray, matplotlib, statsmodels, seaborn, networkx) and found no usage of `np.dot` with a >2D second argument outside of test files. Details posted in #31725.

This PR adds a deprecation warning when `a.ndim >= 2` and `b.ndim > 2`, suggesting `numpy.tensordot(a, b, axes=[-1, -2])` for the same result or `@`/`matmul` for standard batched operations.

**Changes:**
- Created internal `PyArray_MatrixProduct_int()` with `warn_on_interleave` flag, following NumPy's `_int` suffix convention
- All public functions call it directly: `PyArray_MatrixProduct`, `PyArray_MatrixProduct2`, `array_matrixproduct` (np.dot), `array_dot` (ndarray.dot)
- `np.inner` and C extensions call via the public API with `warn=0`
- Warning fires only when `a.ndim >= 2` AND `b.ndim > 2` (actual dimension interleaving)
- Deprecation check runs after shape validation, so shape mismatch raises `ValueError` (not `DeprecationWarning`) even with `-W error`. Also, reusing existing cleanup paths (no redundant conversions).
- Updated `np.dot` docstring with a `.. deprecated:: 2.6` note, and noted the deprecation before the affected example
- Docstring examples still run in the doctest suite: the new warning is added to the doctest ignore list in `numpy/conftest.py` (same as `numpy.fix` and `chararray`), so example output is still checked. Users running the examples still see the warning.
- Added `TestDotDimensionInterleaving` class in `test_deprecations.py` with 7 tests (including shape mismatch priority test)
- Updated `test_dot_errstate` in `test_multiarray.py` and masked array tests in `test_core.py` and `test_extras.py` to expect the warning
- Added release note (`32759.deprecation.rst`)

**Why an internal wrapper?**

The deprecation check was initially placed in `PyArray_MatrixProduct2()`, but `np.inner()` also calls this shared function and should not trigger the warning. Rather than duplicating the matrix product logic, we created an internal implementation with a flag parameter. This avoids code duplication while keeping the warning scoped to `np.dot`/`ndarray.dot` only.

**Lesson learned:** Running `spin test` (the full test suite) locally before pushing catches failures earlier, rather than discovering them in CI. Additionally, running the doctest suite (`spin test -- --doctest-modules --doctest-only-doctests=true --doctest-collect=api`) catches failures in docstring examples that unit tests miss.

#### AI Disclosure

AI assisted with codebase navigation, identifying NumPy conventions for deprecation warnings and tests, and drafting code and documentation. All changes were reviewed and tested locally before submitting.

title: Weird behavior of Numpy.fft in solving a chaotic system
body:
Implementing a numerical scheme of ETDRK4, published in SIAM J.S.C in 2005, cited over 600 times. Trefethen is the God in spectral method. So the algorithm is in high trust. Matlab code is directly in the paper. So there should be no issue with the matlab code. Python code is what I copied from matlab and did some grammar correction. It is also proved to be match perfect. I did numerous sanity checks. 

Matlab gives me stable result.
Scipy.fftpack gives me stable result.
**Numpy.fft gives me blow up.**

See the post here (full code is contained in that post ):
https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/weird-behavior-numpyfft-solving-chaotic-system-shaowu-shawn-pan/

The code with postprocessing is given below. Very short. Trust me.

```
#######################################################################
#
# Showing the difference between numpy.fft and scipy.fft
#
# Author: Shaowu Pan
#
# Date: 02/11/2018
# 
#######################################################################

# import numpy and pyplot
import numpy as np
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
import sys

# try to import numpyr or scipy fft based on argv
if sys.argv[1] == 'numpy':
    ## choose numpy
    from numpy.fft import fft,ifft
else:
    # choose scipy
    from scipy.fftpack import fft, ifft


# define constant
pi = np.pi

# viscosity
nu = 1

# mesh
mesh = 128

# time restriction
tot = 30

# distributed x point
x = np.linspace(0, 2.0 * pi, mesh, endpoint=False)

# force IC
u0 = np.cos(x)*(1.0 + np.sin(x))

# set up mesh grid and k array
N = mesh
k_array_noshift = np.fft.fftfreq(mesh)*mesh

# set up initial condition
u = u0
v = fft(u)

# time step
h = 0.01

## follow them, set -N/2 to zer
k_array_noshift[mesh / 2] = 0

## Linear part in fourier space
L = 1.0/16.0*k_array_noshift**2 - nu*1.0/16.0**3 * k_array_noshift**4

## Fourier mulitplier
E = np.exp(h * L)
E2 = np.exp(h * L / 2.0)

## select number of points on the circle
M = 16

## choose radius 1, since k^2-k^4 ranges a lot... so 1 is enough to make sure only one singular point
r = np.exp(1j * np.pi * (np.arange(1, M + 1) - 0.5) / M)
r = r.reshape(1, -1)
r_on_circle = np.repeat(r, mesh, axis=0)

## define hL on M copies
LR = h * L
LR = LR.reshape(-1, 1)
LR = np.repeat(LR, M, axis=1)

## obtain hL on circle
LR = LR + r_on_circle

## important quantites used in ETDRK4

# g = -0.5*i*k
g = -0.5j * k_array_noshift

# averaged Q, f1,f2,f3
Q = h*np.real(np.mean( (np.exp(LR/2.0)-1)/LR, axis=1 ))

f1 = h*np.real(np.mean( (-4.0-LR + np.exp(LR)*(4.0-3.0*LR+LR**2))/LR**3, axis=1 ))

f2 = h*np.real(np.mean( (2.0+LR + np.exp(LR)*(-2.0 + LR))/LR**3, axis=1 ))

f3 = h*np.real(np.mean( (-4.0-3.0*LR - LR**2 + np.exp(LR)*(4.0 - LR))/LR**3, axis=1 ))


def compute_u2k_zeropad_dealiased(uk_):
    """
    3/2 zero padding de-aliasing
    """
    # u2k = fft(np.real(ifft(uk_))**2)
    # three over two law
    N = uk_.size

    # map uk to uk_fine

    uk_fine = np.hstack((uk_[0:N / 2], np.zeros((N / 2)), uk_[-N / 2:])) * 3.0 / 2.0

    # convert uk_fine to physical space
    u_fine = np.real(ifft(uk_fine))

    # compute square
    u2_fine = np.square(u_fine)

    # compute fft on u2_fine
    u2k_fine = fft(u2_fine)

    # convert u2k_fine to u2k
    u2k = np.hstack((u2k_fine[0:N / 2], u2k_fine[-N / 2:])) / 3.0 * 2.0

    return u2k


print 'dt =', h

# np.linalg.norm(np.fft.ifft(uk_0)-u0) # very good

ntsnap = int(tot/h)
isnap = 0
tsnap = np.linspace(0, tot, ntsnap)
usnap = np.zeros((mesh, ntsnap))
uksnap = np.zeros((mesh, ntsnap),dtype=complex)

aasnap = np.zeros((mesh, ntsnap),dtype=complex)
bbsnap = np.zeros((mesh, ntsnap),dtype=complex)
ccsnap = np.zeros((mesh, ntsnap),dtype=complex)

Nvsnap = np.zeros((mesh, ntsnap),dtype=complex)
Nasnap = np.zeros((mesh, ntsnap),dtype=complex)
Nbsnap = np.zeros((mesh, ntsnap),dtype=complex)
Ncsnap = np.zeros((mesh, ntsnap),dtype=complex)


tcur = 0.0

## main loop time stepping
while tcur <= tot and isnap < ntsnap:

    # print tcur

    # record snap
    # if abs(tcur - tsnap[isnap]) < 1e-2:
    # print ' current progress =', tcur / tsnap[-1] * 100, ' % '
    u = np.real(ifft(v))
    usnap[:, isnap] = u
    uksnap[:, isnap] = v

    # Nv = g * fft(np.real(ifft(v))**2)
    Nv = g * compute_u2k_zeropad_dealiased(v)

    a = E2 * v + Q * Nv

    # Na = g * fft(np.real(ifft(a))**2)
    Na = g * compute_u2k_zeropad_dealiased(a)

    b = E2 * v + Q * Na

    # Nb = g * fft(np.real(ifft(b))**2)
    Nb = g * compute_u2k_zeropad_dealiased(b)

    c = E2 * a + Q * (2.0*Nb - Nv)

    # Nc = g * fft(np.real(ifft(c))**2)
    Nc = g * compute_u2k_zeropad_dealiased(c)

    v = E*v + Nv*f1 + 2.0*(Na + Nb)*f2 + Nc*f3

    aasnap[:, isnap] = a
    bbsnap[:, isnap] = b
    ccsnap[:, isnap] = c

    Nvsnap[:, isnap] = Nv
    Nasnap[:, isnap] = Na
    Nbsnap[:, isnap] = Nb
    Ncsnap[:, isnap] = Nc

    # record time
    tcur = tcur + h
    isnap = isnap + 1

# save uksnap
np.savez('output_uk',uksnap=uksnap,f1=f1,f2=f2,f3=f3,Q=Q,LR=LR,L=L,g=g, Nasnap=Nasnap, Nvsnap=Nvsnap, Nbsnap=Nbsnap, Ncsnap=Ncsnap,
         aasnap=aasnap, bbsnap=bbsnap, ccsnap=ccsnap, usnap=usnap)

# plot contours
from matplotlib import cm

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 8))
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, tsnap)
Z = usnap.transpose()
V = np.linspace(-10, 10, 500)
surf = plt.contourf(X, Y, Z, V, cmap=cm.seismic)
plt.savefig('contour.png')
```

title: BUG: fix result mask placement in np.ma.isin and np.ma.in1d (gh-19877)
body:
`numpy.ma.in1d` currently handles masks incorrectly when the first input
contains masked elements. The membership values themselves are correct, but
the mask on the result can be applied to the wrong positions.

This change makes the membership check operate on the underlying data while
preserving the mask positions from the first input. Masked values in the
second input are also excluded from the set of values used for the membership
check.

`setdiff1d`, which also relies on `in1d`, is updated accordingly so that
masked elements are preserved correctly in its result.

Closes #19877

## Why was this issue selected?

I picked this issue because it is a relatively small but concrete bug in
`numpy.ma` behavior, and it gave me an opportunity to understand how masked
arrays are handled internally. Fixing it also helps make the behavior of
`in1d`/`isin` more consistent when masked data is involved.

## First-time contributor

Hi, I'm Md Imam Hossain. I'm currently studying B.Tech CSE AILML and
mostly use Python for [ML/data analysis/scientific computing/etc.]. I have
been using NumPy as part of my Python work, and this is my first contribution
to the NumPy project.

## Tests

Added a regression test covering masked input to ensure that:

- membership is determined from the underlying data;
- masked positions in the first argument remain masked in the result; and
- masked values in the second argument are not treated as values to match.

The relevant `numpy.ma` tests were run to check for regressions.

title: DOC: add table of which operations return views or copies
body:
### PR summary

Please note that non-maintainers may only have 2 non-draft PRs open for review at a
time.

-->
- What problem does this PR solve? Link any relevant issues and PRs.

This PR is related to [issue 20112](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/20112).
The code aims to document the numpy operations that return views vs copies.
I added a comment to the issue asking some feedback on the approach, I have not heard back so I am submitting in this PR a first version of the documentation to get some feedback and understand if the methodology (explained below) makes sense.

As I was trying to verify the behaviour of different operations I realised that there are some interesting cases which have a different return type depending on the input. I think for those it would be worth adding a snippet of the code showing what happens with different inputs. 
This PR only adds a section in [Copies and views](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.copies.html) with the return types without any code.

#### How each operation was classified

Every entry was checked against a build of current `main`, not taken from the docstrings. Each operation runs on a sample array `x` and produces `y`:

```python
if y is x:                    # the operation handed back its input
    outcome = "same"
elif np.shares_memory(x, y):  # a different array over the same memory
    outcome = "view"
else:
    outcome = "copy"
```

`same` and `view` are both reported as "View", since neither copies data.

I initially used `y.base` as the documentation says: 
"_The `base` attribute of the ndarray makes it easy to tell if an array is a view or a copy. The base attribute of a view returns the original array while it returns None for a copy."_

While testing different cases I saw that checking `.base` might still return `False` when the return is a view that can edit the original array. For example:

```python
x = np.arange(24).reshape(4, 6).copy()

y = x.T.reshape(-1)        # reshape cannot view a transposed array, so it copies
y.base is None             # False: .base says view
np.shares_memory(x, y)     # False: it is a copy

z = np.asarray(x)          # returns x itself, nothing copied
z.base is None             # True: .base says copy
np.shares_memory(x, z)     # True: it is x
```
That is why I decided to use `np.shares_memory`. `.base` was only used for empty results since `np.shares_memory` is `False` even for a view of an empty array.
With this in mind, it might be worth editing [this section ](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.copies.html#how-to-tell-if-the-array-is-a-view-or-a-copy)of the docs too. Let me know if you agree with the approach.

A mix of outcomes is reported as "View or copy", with the note saying what determines it:

- Why are you interested in working on this PR?

Was looking at different open issues an since this is my first contribution I wanted to start with a doc change to get some experience. This issue stood out since understanding which operations share memory with the original array can avoid some unpleasant surprised and clarifies what your code is actually editing.

- How does the proposed change help you?

I am part of the 2026 Sustain cohort, would like to keep contributing to open source, especially numpy-financial.

title: BUG: avoid undefined shift in rational test dtype
body:
## PR summary

TL;DR
This fixes the UBSan-reported undefined shift in `_rational_tests.c` by using NumPy's existing minimum-value constant instead. The corresponding UBSan suppressions for arm64 and x86_64 are removed as they are no longer needed. There is no intended API or behavior change.

Previously, `safe_neg()` used `(npy_int32)1 << 31` to construct the minimum 32-bit signed value, which UBSan reports as undefined behavior. The check now uses `NPY_MIN_INT32`.

This addresses the `_rational_tests.c` `shift-base` item in the UBSan cleanup tracker.

Related:
- Tracking issue: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/29524
- Prior related UBSan shift cleanup: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/29539

Validation with a UBSan build:

- reproduced the UBSan failure before the change and confirmed it no longer occurs afterward;
- `numpy/_core/tests/test_ufunc.py`: 886 passed, 7 expected xfails;
- full default non-slow NumPy suite: 48,592 passed with no failures;

title: Variant analysis: 1 unfixed sibling safety gap in numpy
body:
## Summary

Variant analysis of historical fixes in **numpy** identified **1 code site** where an integer-overflow guard, bounds check, or safe-allocation wrapper exists at one location but is missing at a structurally identical sibling location (same file, same function, or same pattern family) elsewhere in the codebase.

Each finding below is **code-confirmed against the current HEAD** (verified by cloning the repository fresh and checking the pattern is still present), with the exact file/line locations, the root cause, a description of the trigger path, and — where available — ASan/execution verification output or a proof-of-concept.

Note on origin: these were surfaced by an automated variant-analysis pipeline that diffs historical fix commits against sibling code paths, then has each candidate manually reviewed. I'm posting them together per-project rather than as separate issues to respect maintainer time. Happy to split, close, or reprioritize any of these as you see fit.

---

## Finding 1: numpy — `string_add` missing output buffer width check (sibling to fixed `string_multiply`)

*Verified against HEAD: `a98529df (2026-09-25)`*

*- **Project**: numpy (numpy/numpy)
- **Class**: Heap-buffer-overflow write (missing bounds check on fixed-width string output buffer)
- **Status**: Code-confirmed, exec-blocked
- **Sibling of**: Commit `d0de6a1a9` — fixed heap overflow in `string_multiply` by adding output width cap*

**Discovery method**

Variant analysis. Commit `d0de6a1a9` fixed a heap overflow in `string_multiply` where `reps_ > width` caused writes past the output buffer. The fix added `min(reps_, width)` to cap characters written. `string_add` in the **same file** combines two strings without checking whether `len1 + len2` fits in the output buffer width.

**Vulnerable code**

**FIXED** — `string_multiply`, after commit `d0de6a1a9`:
```cpp
size_t end_index = reps_ > width ? width : reps_;  // CAP added
buf1.buffer_memcpy(out, end_index);
out.buffer_fill_with_zeros_after_index(end_index);
```

**UNFIXED** — `string_add`, lines 159-165:
```cpp
static inline void
string_add(Buffer<enc> buf1, Buffer<enc> buf2, Buffer<enc> out)
{
    size_t len1 = buf1.num_codepoints();
    size_t len2 = buf2.num_codepoints();
    buf1.buffer_memcpy(out, len1);                          // NO width check
    buf2.buffer_memcpy(out + len1, len2);                   // NO width check
    out.buffer_fill_with_zeros_after_index(len1 + len2);    // NO width check
}
```

No check that `len1 + len2 <= out.buffer_width()`. When called from `string_add_loop` at line 217-243 with `outsize = context->descriptors[2]->elsize`, normal ufunc dispatch correctly sizes the output via `string_addition_resolve_descriptors` (line 735-776) which computes `result_itemsize = descr1->elsize + descr2->elsize`. **However**, when using `out=` (in-place or pre-allocated output), the output descriptor retains its original size, creating a mismatch.

**Root cause**

The `string_multiply` fix added a cap (`min(reps_, width)`) to prevent write past the output buffer. `string_add` has the same vulnerability — `len1 + len2` can exceed `out.buffer_width()` — but was not fixed with the same pattern. The normal dispatch path computes correct output size, but the `out=` argument short-circuits this.

**Concrete example**

```python
import numpy as np
a = np.array(['hello'], dtype='S5')  # fixed-width 5-byte strings
b = np.array(['world'], dtype='S5')
# 'hello' + 'world' = 10 bytes, but out=a is only 5 bytes wide
np.add(a, b, out=a)  # writes 10 bytes into 5-byte buffer → heap overflow
```

The `buffer_memcpy` copies `len1=5` bytes to `out`, then `len2=5` bytes to `out + 5`. If `out` is only 5 bytes wide, the second memcpy writes 5 bytes past the allocation.

**Trigger path**

1. User (or fuzzer) creates fixed-width string arrays with narrow width
2. → Calls `np.add(a, b, out=a)` where combined string length exceeds output width
3. → `string_add` is called with output buffer width < len1 + len2
4. → `buffer_memcpy(out + len1, len2)` writes past end of output allocation
5. → Heap overflow, potentially corrupting adjacent numpy array data

**Fuzz harness**: Standard numpy fuzzer or hypothesis-based property test with `out=` parameter on string operations.

**Sibling-gap quality**

**Excellent.** Same file (`string_ufuncs.cpp`), same class of bug, same mechanism (fixed-width string buffer width vs. operation result width mismatch), same mitigation pattern needed. The `string_multiply` fix proves the developers recognized this class of bug; `string_add` was simply missed.

---

*Analysis date: 2026-09-22. Code-confirmed, not execution-verified.*

---

## Methodology

For each historical vulnerability fix in the codebase, we identified the safe pattern the fix introduced (an overflow guard, a safe allocator wrapper, a bounds check) and searched the rest of the codebase for structurally identical code that predates or postdates the fix but never received it. Each candidate was then manually verified against the current HEAD listed above.

Happy to provide anything else that would help triage — additional PoC inputs, a minimal patch following the existing safe-sibling pattern, or a written reproduction script.

title: BUG: ndarray.__reduce__ converts shape errors to SystemError
body:
### Describe the issue:

`ndarray.__reduce__()` does not propagate exceptions raised by a subclass's `shape` property.

In `array_reduce()`, the result of `PyObject_GetAttrString(self, "shape")` is passed directly to `PyTuple_SET_ITEM()` without checking for `NULL`. If the attribute access raises, `array_reduce()` can return a non-NULL result while an exception is still set, which results in `SystemError`.

This is reproducible with an `ndarray` subclass that overrides `shape`.

### Reproduce the code example:

```python
import numpy as np
import pickle


class BadArray(np.ndarray):
    @property
    def shape(self):
        raise RuntimeError("bad shape")


arr = np.array([1, 2, 3]).view(BadArray)

arr.__reduce__()
```

### Error message:

```shell
SystemError: <method '__reduce__' of 'numpy.ndarray' objects> returned a result with an exception set
```

### Python and NumPy Versions:

Python 3.12.6
NumPy 2.6.0.dev0+git20260925.b40d1b4

### Runtime Environment:

Windows 64-bit

### How does this issue affect you or how did you find it:

This was found while triaging a C-extension audit reported in this gist:
https://gist.github.com/devdanzin/ccc2d9553ca1c90ab1835362ee21a40a8

After checking the finding against current main, I reproduced it with an ndarray subclass overriding shape. A local null check for the shape lookup makes the original RuntimeError propagate correctly through both __reduce__() and pickle.dumps().

I'm opening this issue first to confirm the expected behavior before preparing a fix.

title: Reciprocal of complex 0 and `1 / numpy.array(0+0j)` give different results
body:
`numpy.reciprocal(a)` and `1 / a` give different results with `a = numpy.array(0 + 0j)`. `reciprocal` gives `nan+nanj`, and `1 / a` gives `inf+nanj`.

It seems like neither of these results is correct, but I could certainly be wrong. I feel like the result in both cases should be `inf+0j`, since we get `inf` when we use real numbers: `1 / numpy.array(0.0)` and `numpy.reciprocal(numpy.array(0.0))`.


### Reproducing code example:

<!-- A short code example that reproduces the problem/missing feature. It should be
self-contained, i.e., possible to run as-is via 'python myproblem.py' -->


```
>>> import numpy

>>> a = numpy.array(0 + 0j)
__main__:1: RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in reciprocal
>>> numpy.reciprocal(a)
(nan+nanj)
>>> 1 / a
(inf+nanj)

>>> 1 / numpy.array(0.0)
inf
>>> numpy.reciprocal(numpy.array(0.0))
__main__:1: RuntimeWarning: divide by zero encountered in reciprocal
inf
```

title: DOC: Improve fromstring documentation & errors/warnings regarding binary mode

labels.name: sustain-2026
labels.description: Issues reserved for NumFOCUS Sustaining Open Source Series 2026

body:
### Issue with current documentation:

I was trying to convert a string '3' to `np.dtypes.Int64DType`. 

My first attempt was `np.dtypes.Int64DType('3')`, hoping that the dtype would be callable which it is not.

Then followed these attempts:
```python
dt = numpy.dtypes.Int64DType
dt('3')  # I was somewhat hoping this would work but the dtype is not callable
np.fromstring('3', dtype=dt)  # ValueError: string size must be a multiple of element size
np.fromstring('3', dtype=dt, count=1)  # ValueError: string is smaller than requested size
np.fromstring('[3]', dtype=dt, count=1)  # ValueError: Cannot create an object array from a string
```

For the latter three calls, I also got a `<string>:1: DeprecationWarning: The binary mode of fromstring is deprecated, as it behaves surprisingly on unicode inputs. Use frombuffer instead` - which I did not understand, because
- '3' is not a binary string
- I did not see a "binary mode" flag or anything of the sort

It took me a long time to realize that the deprecated *default optional argument* `sep=''` was causing this behavior. I personally find this highly unintuitive and surprising. (I did not look at this argument at all because I was interested in the scalar case.)

Indeed, `np.fromstring('3', dtype=int, sep=' ')`at least works.

However,  `np.fromstring('3', dtype=np.dtypes.Int64DType, sep=' ')`gives `ValueError: Cannot create an object array from a string` - which I again find surprising.

### Idea or request for content:

At the very least, I would suggest adding a note to the deprecation warning that the binary mode is triggered by the default optional argument `sep=''`, and that passing any other value to `sep` will fix the issue.

In addition, I would suggest adding some comment to the documentation on why passing things like `dtype=numpy.dtypes.Int64DType` does not work.

In addition, I would suggest adding a comment that `np.array(str, dtype=...)` might be what one is looking for.

title: DOC/TYP: weird new behaviour around `timedelta64` after 2.5.0
body:
### Describe the issue:

After 2.5.0, `np.dtype("timedelta64[...]")` becomes more detailed but new behaviours are sometimes confusing. Discovered while trying to resolve pandas-dev/pandas-stubs#1786.

### Reproduce the code example:

```python
from typing import reveal_type
import numpy as np

reveal_type(np.dtype("timedelta64[ns]"))  # static: dtype[timedelta64[int]]
reveal_type(np.dtype("timedelta64[s]"))  # static: dtype[timedelta64[timedelta]]
reveal_type(np.dtype("timedelta64[Y]"))  # static: dtype[timedelta64[int]]
```

### Error message:

```shell
It is not so easy to understand 2 giving `timedelta64[timedelta]`, while 1 and 3 gives `timedelta64[int]` (not monotonic).
```
